title: Lazarus Saturday
hook: the Orthodox celebrate Lazarus raised, the day before Palm Sunday

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mothering Sunday: back to the mother church, then to your mother's door. Your line was go home.

A message reaches Jesus from two sisters in Bethany, Mary and Martha. In the King James Bible it's one line: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Their brother Lazarus. And Jesus waits two more days. By the time he reaches Bethany, Lazarus has been in the grave four days. Martha comes out to meet him on the road, later Mary falls at his feet, and each says the same sentence: if you had been here, my brother would not have died. Then Jesus stands before a cave with a stone across it and asks for the stone to be rolled away. Martha, practical to the end, warns him about the smell. On the Saturday before Palm Sunday, Orthodox Christians tell this whole story again.

John tells this one slowly, and three short lines carry it. The first is two words long: "Jesus wept." He stands with the sisters at the grave, and he weeps. John doesn't skip the grief to hurry on to the miracle, and neither does Jesus. The second is a shout. In the King James: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man comes out, still bound hand and foot in grave clothes, his face wrapped in a cloth. The third is easy to miss. Jesus turns to the people standing around and says: "Loose him, and let him go." Jesus calls him out; everyone else has to do the unwrapping. Coming back takes a voice, and then a lot of ordinary hands working at knots. Why keep it on this Saturday? Because John sets the two scenes side by side. Right after Bethany, he says, a crowd that had heard about Lazarus took palm branches and went out to meet Jesus on the road into Jerusalem. So Orthodox churches treat this day as a hinge between Lent and Holy Week, a preview of Easter: the one who calls his friend out of a tomb is about to walk toward his own. And John adds a hard detail. After the raising, the chief priests talk about putting Lazarus to death as well. Being called out of the grave didn't make his life safe. It made it visible.

Bring to mind someone who came back from something: an illness, a dark year, a long silence. Picture their face at the worst point and the way it looks now, then think about the hands that helped unwrap them; maybe yours were among them. If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if not, simply hold them in mind, glad they came out.
Lazarus Saturday. The day before Palm Sunday, when Orthodox Christians remember Jesus calling his friend out of the tomb at Bethany.
Your line: come out. A voice first, then many hands. That's day one thousand twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians keep Lazarus Saturday the day before Palm Sunday, with a service that retells John 11 and, in some places, by making palm crosses or special breads for the next day.

fork.setup: you're Martha. Jesus is standing at your brother's tomb, four days too late, and he asks for the stone to be rolled away. what do you say?

fork.reveal: practical Martha warns him about the smell. Jesus answers that if she believes she will see the glory of God, and the stone is moved.

chat.says: Why do Orthodox Christians remember Lazarus right before Palm Sunday?
options: John puts them side by side: the crowd with palms had heard about Lazarus.
Lazarus was the man who led the donkey into Jerusalem that Sunday.
It's when Lazarus died, so they mourn him before the Easter joy.
chat.meaning: In John, a crowd that heard about Lazarus took palm branches to meet Jesus. So the day is a hinge into Holy Week, a preview of Easter.
